title: FG% and FT% Anchors and Liabilities
brief: Which players move our team FG% and FT% most, up or down, given their shot volume? It must note that percentages are team ratios driven by attempts and that FT% is the least stable category year to year.
summary: FG% and FT% are team ratios, so the players who move them most combine an extreme percentage with high attempts. Low-volume efficiency barely counts. FT% is the least stable category from year to year, so price shooters on their norm, not on one season. Pick one percentage to protect before the 2026-10-18 auction instead of chasing both.

paragraphs.text: In our league, FG% and FT% are team ratios: total makes divided by total attempts for the week. A player's percentage counts in proportion to how many shots he takes. Good efficiency on low volume does not matter much. So judge a shooter by his gap from average multiplied by his attempts, not by his percentage alone.

Here is an example. A center who makes 72 percent of a few shots a game helps you less than a big man who makes 57 percent on 18 attempts. In the same way, a 41 percent foul shooter who takes 2 free throws a game does little harm, while a 64 percent shooter on 10 or more attempts sinks the category. Rate stats also have no floor. A bad volume shooter keeps pulling your team down every game he plays.

sections.heading: FT% is the least stable category

paragraphs.text: Regress shooting percentages in your projections. Year-to-year correlations are 0.53 for two-point percentage, 0.52 for true shooting, 0.49 for free throw percentage and 0.45 for three-point percentage. FT% is now the least stable of the standard fantasy categories. FG% varies most from game to game and week to week.

Surprise free throw swings in either direction usually fade and drift back toward the player's norm. You cannot predict them. So do not call a player a bad shooter as a fixed fact. Say how he shot last season. Only extreme cases, like Giannis at the free throw line, are close to certain.

What to do at the auction: price FT% anchors and liabilities on their usual level, not on last season alone. Do not pay extra for a player whose FT% jumped. Do not write off one whose FT% dropped. During the season, do not spend FAB on a waiver player because of a hot free throw start. Do not drop a proven FT% anchor after a cold few weeks.

Being strong in both FG% and FT% is very hard. Barely winning both is fragile, and spending resources on both leaves you short in other categories. Decide before the 2026-10-18 auction which percentage you protect and which one you will give up.

Most anchors here help one percentage and hurt the other. The tiers below mark each player as an FG% or FT% anchor or liability and, where it applies, as mixed. A punt FT% team can stack big men who are FG% anchors and FT% liabilities. A punt FG% team can stack volume guards whose FG% hurts but whose FT% helps. Ignore low-volume efficiency in either direction when you set prices.
Giannis is the clearest case. His FT% weakness on heavy volume is close to certain. If you buy him, commit to punting FT% and do not spend more money trying to save the category.

Percentages are not safe in low-volume weeks. With fewer attempts, each miss moves the ratio more, so results swing more. Check how many games your shooters play in each week, especially in playoff weeks 19 to 21. A two-game week for your key anchor makes the category less certain.

Because shooting stats have no floor, you can lose a lead in FG% or FT% on the last day of a matchup. We set lineups daily. On the final day, if you hold a narrow lead in a percentage, think about benching a high-volume liability. First weigh what he would add in points, threes or assists.
